name: Lip repositioning surgery

lead: Lip repositioning surgery is aimed at gummy smiles caused by an upper lip that rises too far. It limits how high the lip lifts, so less gum shows and the smile looks more balanced.

A strip of mucosa is removed from inside the upper lip and the lip is reattached in a lower position, which reduces the depth of the vestibule and may increase lip fullness. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis measured the short- and long-term reduction in gum display, and the research base is mainly case series and small trials.

paras: It is an elective procedure done by a dental or oral surgeon, with the reduced gum display visible after healing. Technique variations such as adding a myotomy are discussed in the literature. People choose it when lip movement, rather than the gum line, is the cause.
It is a surgical procedure with the usual healing period. Reviews and trials examine relapse, meaning the lip can drift back up over time, and technique choices that affect it.

angle.text: Lip repositioning is used for gummy smiles caused by a hypermobile upper lip. A strip of inner lip mucosa is removed and the lip reattached lower, limiting how far it rises on smiling. The reduced gum display is visible after healing.

lead: Lip repositioning surgery (LRS) is a procedure for excessive gingival display, commonly called a gummy smile, in which strips of mucosa are removed from the inside of the upper lip and the lip is stitched back in a more coronal position, so that it rises less far when the person smiles.[1][2] People seek it to show a smaller band of gum and more of the teeth and lip in photographs and in everyday expression; one description adds that the repositioning also increases lip fullness.[2] It is used particularly when a hypermobile upper lip is a cause.[3]

Gummy smile has several possible origins, which may occur alone or together: delayed passive eruption of the teeth, overactive lip elevator muscles, excessive vertical growth of the upper jaw and over-eruption of the upper front teeth.[4][5] Because each cause calls for a different treatment, clinicians describe a diagnostic work-up before choosing between lip repositioning, crown lengthening, botulinum toxin, orthodontics or jaw surgery.[5][3] Reviews place LRS as a relatively simple, conservative option for patients with increased lip mobility and mild vertical maxillary excess.[6][5]

Published work includes case series, small randomized trials and systematic reviews. A 2021 meta-analysis quantified reduction in gum display over 3, 6 and 12 months and examined the effect of myotomy,[7] and several registered trials are comparing modified techniques and ways of limiting relapse.[8][9][10][11]

With or without myotomy or frenectomy; laser-assisted; modified suturing

paras: One description states that LRS involves precise resection of maxillary mucosal tissue with reattachment of the lip in a more coronal position, which restricts lip elevation on smiling and increases lip fullness.[2] The shallower vestibule means the elevator muscles can still move the lip, but its upper border meets the gum line sooner.[1][12] Reviews of the technique describe it as a procedure that has been modified many times since its original description roughly fifty years ago.[6]

A 2023 narrative review identifies altered passive eruption and lip hypermobility as the two major soft-tissue causes of gummy smile, with aesthetic crown lengthening and lip repositioning as the established surgical options for each.[3] Where more than one cause is present, the two can be staged or combined, as in a published case of a teenager with altered passive eruption and a hyperactive lip.[13][14]

Variations reported in the literature include adding a myotomy or muscle-containment step, a frenectomy, full- versus partial-thickness flaps, and dual-layer suturing.[15][16][17] Laser-assisted versions use a laser in place of a scalpel for the tissue removal.[18] A modified technique that ties the levator labii superioris without frenectomy or myotomy has been evaluated in a registered retrospective study.[19] Another registered trial compares a milled PEEK stent with lip repositioning, and one compares lip repositioning with Z-plasty.[8][9]
A 2013 case series described a reversible trial in which patients could preview the outcome before the permanent operation.[2]

The 2021 meta-analysis of studies using LRS alone found a mean reduction in gum display of 2.87 mm at 3 months, 2.71 mm at 6 months and 2.10 mm at 12 months, and described a progressive decrease over time consistent with partial relapse; myotomy was associated with greater reduction at 6 months.[7] A separate meta-analysis of 38 studies, mostly case reports and case series, compared combinations of frenectomy, flap thickness and myotomy and reported reductions of roughly 2.9 mm at 6 months for a frenectomy, full-thickness flap and myotomy combination.[15]

A systematic review of 144 patients aged 15 to 59 (mostly women) concluded that lip repositioning with myotomy or muscle containment can be successful for minor discrepancies in gum display in selected cases, while recommending controlled trials to establish long-term stability.[17] A 2022 review of techniques reports high patient satisfaction and improved smile aesthetics when the procedure is applied to properly diagnosed cases.[6]

In a study using photographs rated by 100 observers, the perceived attractiveness of smiles was assessed before and six months after aesthetic crown lengthening or lip repositioning.[14] A 3-year prospective study in twins has also been published for a modified approach.[20]

A 2022 review characterises LRS as a relatively simple procedure with minimal complications,[6] and the 2024 Cureus review calls it minimally invasive.[5] The main outcome studied in follow-up is relapse, the gradual return of lip elevation toward its preoperative level.[7][21] Studies have also measured lip dimensional changes at six months, since the repositioned lip can appear fuller or tighter.[12] As with any intraoral surgery, swelling, discomfort and healing time are part of recovery, and registered trials are testing liquid fibrin and low-level laser as healing aids.[11]

Botulinum toxin injected into the lip elevator muscles is a widely described non-surgical alternative that reduces upward lip movement for an average of about six months.[4] Crown lengthening addresses gum excess when altered passive eruption is the cause, and orthodontics or orthognathic surgery address skeletal or dental causes.[3][4]

Botulinum toxin has also been tested as an adjunct to lip repositioning. A randomized trial of 18 participants injected the smile muscles 15 days before surgery in the test group to see whether this would stabilise the result,[21] and a second randomized trial of 22 patients used relapse as its primary outcome.[22] A published case describes repeated toxin injections combined with LRS.[10]

Published studies include a case series of seven patients with a reversible trial,[2] a staged case report combining crown lengthening and LRS,[13] a smile-attractiveness study after crown lengthening and LRS,[14] a 6-month lip-dimension study,[12] a 3-year twin study,[20] and the meta-analyses and systematic reviews described above.[7][17][15]

Two randomized trials have examined botulinum toxin before LRS, one with 18 and one with 22 participants.[21][22] Registered trials compare modified techniques, PEEK stents, Z-plasty, Botox pretreatment and healing aids.[8][9][10][11] Reviewers note that much of the evidence consists of case reports and small series and call for larger controlled trials.[17][15]
